summary: DHCP clients may try to update the same DNS name or one added for another purpose, causing conflicts. To resolve them, RFC 4703 proposes storing client identifiers in the DNS. This memo defines the DHCID resource record type for that purpose. It was later updated by RFC 5494.

eli5.summary: When two computers both claim the same name in the phone book, you need a way to tell who it really belongs to. This adds a tag in the DNS recording which computer owns the name.

questions: dns record for dhcp client identifier
how is the dhcid hash computed
how do dhcp and dns avoid name conflicts
subtitle: A DNS record that stores a hashed DHCP client identity next to a name, so updaters can tell whose name it is.

tldr.problem: When DHCP clients or servers update DNS automatically, several clients may want the same name, or a name may already exist for another purpose, and nothing in the DNS says who owns it.
tldr.mechanism: The DHCID record (type code 49) holds a 2-octet identifier type, a 1-octet digest type and a SHA-256 hash of the client's identifier plus the domain name.
tldr.outcome: Updaters compare the stored hash with one they compute and, if it differs, treat the name as belonging to another client and follow site policy. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 4701 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 5494. The text of this RFC is not obsoleted by any later RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why DHCP Needs a DNS Record
sections.content:
DHCP clients and servers can update the DNS automatically as clients obtain leases. RFC 4703 describes the procedures. Conflicts arise when several DHCP clients want the same name, or when a client tries to use a name that was added to the DNS for another purpose.

To settle such conflicts, RFC 4703 proposes storing client identifiers in the DNS. This memo defines a distinct record type for that, the DHCID RR, so the DHCP-specific data is clearly separate from other records.

The stored data is the output of a one-way SHA-256 hash, which obscures sensitive client identifying information. The hash also covers the domain name, so the same client gets different data for each name it uses. That makes it hard to track a client across names.
sections.eli5: When two kids want the same cubby, you need a way to see who already has it. The DHCID record is a hidden code on the cubby that shows who owns it without spelling out their name.

sections.title: The DHCID Record Format
sections.content:
The record has mnemonic DHCID and type code 49. It is defined only in the IN class and causes no additional section processing.

DNS software treats the RDATA as opaque. To an updater, the RDATA is a 2-octet identifier type in network byte order, a 1-octet digest type, and one or more octets of digest.

In DNS master files the RDATA is written as a single block of base-64. It may be split into any number of white-space-separated pieces, which are joined together, and it may span lines using parentheses.
sections.eli5: The record is a small label with three parts: what kind of ID was used, which scrambling method was used, and the scrambled code itself. The phone book just copies the label without reading it.

sections.title: Identifier Type and Digest Type Codes
sections.content:
The identifier type code says which piece of the client's DHCP request went into the hash. Three values are assigned: 0x0000 for the 1-octet htype followed by hlen octets of chaddr from a DHCPv4 DHCPREQUEST, 0x0001 for the data octets of a DHCPv4 Client Identifier option, and 0x0002 for the client's DUID. The values 0x0003 to 0xfffe are available to be assigned by IANA, and 0xffff is reserved.

The digest type code names the hash algorithm. Value 0 is reserved and value 1 is SHA-256. Reserving other types requires IETF standards action, and defining new values will also require standards action to document how DNS updaters deal with multiple digest types.
sections.eli5: The first code says what you used to make the secret code (like your name tag or your desk number). The second code says which scrambling machine you used.

sections.title: Computing the RDATA
sections.content:
For every identifier type except the reserved 0xffff, the RDATA is the 2-octet identifier type, the 1-octet digest type and the digest value, which is 32 octets for SHA-256. The digest is SHA-256(< identifier > < FQDN >), where the FQDN is in canonical wire format.

An updater picks the identifier type like this. A DHCPv4 updater uses 0x0002 if a Client Identifier option is present and encoded as specified in RFC 4361. Otherwise it uses 0x0001 if a Client Identifier option is present, and 0x0000 if not. A DHCPv6 updater always uses 0x0002.

With the link-layer address (0x0000), the hash input is the one-octet htype, then the significant octets of chaddr (as many as hlen says), then the FQDN. In each case the first two octets of the record MUST be the identifier type, and the third is the digest type, 1 for SHA-256.
sections.eli5: You take your ID and the name you want, mix them together in a blender (the hash), and write down the result. Anyone with the same ID and name gets the same result, but nobody can un-blend it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. In the first, a server allocates an IPv6 address to a client that sent DHCPv6 client-identifier option data, and updates chi6.example.com on its behalf. The type octets are 0x0002 and the hash covers the 14 octets from the option plus the FQDN.

In the second, a server allocates 192.0.2.2 to a client with DHCP client-identifier option data, and updates chi.example.com. The type is 0x0001 and the hash covers seven octets from the option plus the name.

In the third, the client is identified by its Ethernet MAC address, so the type octets are zero and the hash covers the htype value 0x01, the six MAC octets and client.example.com. Each example also shows the record in the generic \# 35 form for software that does not know the type.
sections.eli5: The examples show three different kids using three different kinds of ID, each ending up with their own secret code on their own name.

sections.title: How Updaters Use the Record
sections.content:
The record lets an updater find out whether more than one DHCP client wants a particular FQDN. It sets no policy itself; site administrators decide that.

An updater computes the client identity hash from the client's request and the desired name, then compares it with the data in any DHCID records on that name. If the data does not match, the updater SHOULD conclude that a different client is currently associated with the name, and SHOULD then follow the site's administrative policy. That policy might pick a different name, or might let the updater continue.

The record MUST NOT be used for any purpose other than the one in RFC 4703. Because the data must be consistent across all entities that update and interpret it, new data formats may only be defined by the DHC Working Group, by revising RFC 4703.
sections.eli5: Before taking a desk, you compare the code on it with your own. If the codes differ, someone else sits there, and you follow the class rules: pick another desk or carry on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The record does not introduce new security problems into the DNS. The one-way hash hides the client's identity, and including the FQDN makes it hard to track a client by the names tied to one hash value.

An attacker who knows something about likely identifiers, such as commonly used MAC addresses, may be able to discover the client's identity by brute force. The number of unknown bits in the hash is typically only 48 to 80.

Administrators should be wary of allowing unsecured DNS updates to zones. Both DHCP clients and servers SHOULD use some form of update authentication, for example TSIG, when performing updates.
sections.eli5: The secret code hides your name, but if a sneaky person can guess which names are likely, they can try them all. So lock the phone book so only the right people can change it.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA allocated a DNS RR type number for DHCID. The memo also creates two new number spaces with registries: the 2-octet identifier type codes and the 1-octet digest type codes. Three initial identifier values are assigned and 0xFFFF is reserved; two initial digest values are assigned. New values in either registry are assigned through Standards Action.
sections.eli5: There are now two official lists, one for kinds of ID and one for scrambling methods. Adding to them takes a formal vote-like process.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF DHCID RDATA

items.title: Identifier type
items.text: 2 octets, network byte order. Says what client data was hashed.

items.title: Digest
items.text: Hash of the identifier plus the FQDN; 32 octets for SHA-256.

items.label: htype and chaddr
items.desc: The 1-octet htype followed by hlen octets of chaddr from a DHCPv4 DHCPREQUEST.

items.label: Client Identifier option
items.desc: The Type and Client-Identifier fields of a DHCPv4 Client Identifier option.

items.label: DUID
items.desc: The client's DUID, from DHCPv6 or from an RFC 4361-encoded DHCPv4 option.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Available to be assigned by IANA.
